slot.brief: Ask why aryl/vinyl halides fail in Williamson synthesis, or which of the given haloalkane + alkoxide pairs gives ether cleanly vs elimination; test the conceptual condition.

stem: Which of the following combinations of a halo-compound and an alkoxide cleanly yields an ether as the major product via Williamson synthesis?

verdicts.working: Williamson synthesis needs SN2 at an unhindered sp3 carbon. (A) 3° t-BuBr with CH3O⁻ gives E2 elimination (isobutene) as major product. (B) Aryl bromide and (D) vinyl bromide are inert to SN2 (sp2 C–X, partial double-bond character). (C) CH3I is a methyl halide; even bulky t-BuO⁻ attacks it by SN2 (no β-H on CH3I, so elimination impossible), cleanly giving methyl tert-butyl ether.

working:
Williamson ether synthesis involves an $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ displacement of a halide ion by an alkoxide/phenoxide nucleophile:
$$\text{R-O}^- + \text{R}'-\text{X} \rightarrow \text{R-O-R}' + \text{X}^-$$

1. In $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CONa} + \text{CH}_3\text{I}$:
   The substrate is a methyl halide ($\text{CH}_3\text{I}$), which lacks $\beta$-hydrogens. Consequently, $\text{E}2$ elimination is structurally impossible. Even though tert-butoxide is a bulky and strongly basic alkoxide, substitution proceeds smoothly via $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ to yield tert-butyl methyl ether as the major product:
   $$(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-O}^- + \text{CH}_3\text{I} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-O-CH}_3 + \text{I}^-$$

2. In $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr} + \text{CH}_3\text{ONa}$:
   The substrate is a tertiary halide ($3^\circ$). Alkoxides are strong bases, so $\text{E}2$ elimination completely outcompetes substitution, yielding 2-methylpropene (isobutylene) exclusively:
   $$(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-Br} + \text{CH}_3\text{O}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_2{=}\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2 + \text{CH}_3\text{OH} + \text{Br}^-$$

3. In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{ONa}$:
   Bromobenzene is an aryl halide. The lone pairs of the bromine atom are delocalized into the aromatic ring by resonance, imparting partial double-bond character to the $\text{C-Br}$ bond. Furthermore, backside $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ attack is geometrically blocked by the benzene ring. Hence, no reaction takes place under standard conditions.

4. In $\text{CH}_2{=}\text{CHBr} + \text{CH}_3\text{ONa}$:
   Vinyl bromide is a vinyl halide. Similar to aryl halides, resonance gives the $\text{C-Br}$ bond partial double-bond character and the $sp^2$-hybridized carbon resists $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ substitution.

Therefore, only combination (C) cleanly yields the ether as the major product.

Independent check: Williamson synthesis needs SN2 at an unhindered sp3 carbon. (A) 3° t-BuBr with CH3O⁻ gives E2 elimination (isobutene) as major product. (B) Aryl bromide and (D) vinyl bromide are inert to SN2 (sp2 C–X, partial double-bond character). (C) CH3I is a methyl halide; even bulky t-BuO⁻ attacks it by SN2 (no β-H on CH3I, so elimination impossible), cleanly giving methyl tert-butyl ether.

draft.distractor_notes:
A: Mistakenly assumes tertiary halides undergo Williamson substitution, overlooking that strong alkoxide bases cause exclusive E2 elimination to 2-methylpropene.
